sections.heading: Abstract
sections.text:
A bistable piezoelectric energy harvester (PEH) is presented for harvesting power from vibrations occurring at low frequencies, as is the case of wind turbine blades. The axial compressive prestress of a piezoelectric composite beam at post-buckling serves as the bistability source, leading to high mechanical to electric power conversion. An in-house harvesting circuit connected to the piezoelectric terminals is used for demonstration of its harvesting power capabilities. A finite element (FE) model is used to analyze and optimize the coupled nonlinear electromechanical response of the PEH, including structure and circuit. A physical prototype has been manufactured and tested for validation of the electromechanical design and the FE modeling approach. Predictions and measurements indicate an increase of harvested power with applied prestress up to a transition point, where a sudden drop in power occurs. Good comparison between numerical and experimental results verified the modeling approach, whereas deviations related to physical boundary conditions at large compressive forces affected the prediction of the transition point in harvested power. The harvester produced $1 . 3 2 \mathrm { m W }$ of electrical power under tonal base excitation of $1 \mathrm { g }$ at $8 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ . Hence, the nonlinear PEH has demonstrated its capability to harvest energy at frequencies much lower than its first linear modal frequency and could thus serve as a promising solution for powering IoT devices and sensors in large vibrating structures.

Keywords: piezoelectric, energy harvesting, finite element, bistability, portable demonstrator, multiphysics simulation, ground test

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Nonlinear piezoelectric energy harvesters (PEH) attract major attention in the emerging field of self-powered systems in the context of the Internet of Things era. Their superiority compared to linear harvesters is attributed to being highly effective in terms of power output over a broad-range of excitation frequencies, while preserving stability in the case of a multistable response [1]. The power harvested through an appropriately tuned circuit is in the $\mathrm { m W }$ range and can thus feed batteries to provide energy to transmitters of sensor network data to the cloud. To that end, numerous multi-stable devices have been designed for harvesting energy from vibrations in several application sectors, such as infrastructure [1, 2], medical [3], wearables [4] to mention a few, while extensive literature reviews provide a detailed overview of the reported research and development in the field [5–9]. The functional principle of a large part of these nonlinear devices is based on electromagnetic forces acting on a cantilever beam carrying piezoelectric transducers [10–12] connected to harvesting circuits [13, 14]. Another popular relevant physical concept is the exploitation of the bistable response of a post-buckled piezoelectric beam subjected to base excitation [15]. The PEH presented in this work is based on the latter concept, while designed for powering-up wireless data transfer systems in wind turbine blades [16].

The electromechanical nonlinear dynamic coupling of a prestressed piezoelectric beam seems to reach its peak in the post-buckling regime and may be tuned in order to achieve maximum performance in terms of output power for a specified frequency and base acceleration input range. The limits of the harvesting design range may be determined through methodologies, such as the one reported by Hosseinloo and Turitsyn for a simple spring-mass-damper system [17], or by using the harmonic balance method to distinguish between intra- and interwell motion of the vibrating prestressed structure [15]. Basic tuning parameters are the axial prestress and the mass of the harvester, the effect of which is predicted by modeling the beam-piezoelectric transducer-harvesting circuit system within specialty developed design tools [18]. In this context, Masana and Daqaq extended the Galerkin formulation and nonlinear Bernoulli beam kinematics of Emam and Nayfeh [19] to axially loaded beams with piezoelectric transducers and demonstrated that tuning of the axial prestress leads to increase of effective bandwidth, output power and electric damping of the system [20]. In subsequent works, the same authors emphasized the significance of shallow potential wells in the energy function distribution with respect to the axial compressive displacement [21] and the role of superharmonic resonance bands [22] for maximizing the effectiveness of the harvester in frequency ranges around one half of the linear eigenfrequency of the beam. Cottone et al developed a Lagrangian formulation with first-order shear theory kinematics to derive a Duffing-like lumped-parameter model for a thin piezoelectric axially loaded beam. They predicted and measured the effect of base acceleration magnitude and prestress on output power and reported an order of magnitude increase in the buckled beam compared to the pre-buckling stage [23]. A lumped spring-mass model has been formulated and experimentally validated by Liu et al for a flexible hinged axially compressed PEH system subjected to chirp and noise excitations [24]. Ansari and Karami designed a PEH including a frame supporting a steel sheet with piezoelectric layers or patches, which buckles in a direct vertical or an indirect horizontal configuration and can produce power in the order of mWatts from passing car traffic [25]. Wu and Xu applied a nonlinear force customization using a raceway at the free end of an axially prestressed specimen to achieve mono-, bi- and tri-stable response at swept-sine base excitation of $5 \mathrm { - } 1 8 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ and base acceleration of $0 . 8 ~ \mathrm { g }$ [26]. Osinaga et al developed a Galerkin-type analytical solution for piezoelectric beams modeled with Euler–Bernoulli through-thickness kinematics in pre- and post-buckling, while considering inertia, damping and piezoelectric nonlinearities, and validated with experimental results [27]. Wang et al developed a bistable energy harvester with piezopolymer transducers and verified predictions of a lumped-parameter model regarding the effect of excitation frequency and acceleration on the type of oscillation experimentally [28].

In the works referenced in the previous paragraph a resistive electric load has been used to indicate the power harvesting capability of post-buckled piezoelectric beam configurations and its superiority compared to linear devices. However, for harvesting part of the mechanical to electric energy conversion occurring via the piezoelectric transducer, the circuits implemented include a rectification stage and electronic subcomponents, such as capacitors and MOSFETS [29–32]. Various in-depth studies of the circuit-structure interaction in the case of bistable mechanical vibrations have been reported in the last decade [33–39], which provide quantitative estimations of harvested power. The mechanical design of these devices is mostly based on lumped-parameter modeling of the coupled nonlinear electromechanical dynamic system. However, the design of durable PEH for implementation in operational environments requires accurate prediction of mechanical stresses and strains at various locations of the harvester, including the vicinity of the supports and transducerhost structure interface. Finite element (FE) models comply to such a requirement, since they predict both the global power output and local distribution of stresses. Yet, existing FE models have been developed for linear PEH [40, 41], for studying transducer material and circuit non-linearities [42, 43], as well as for simulating the mechanical part of the harvester uncoupled from the harvesting circuit [44].

The current work extends current state of the art in PEH design by presenting: A FE-based design process of a nonlinear PEH exploiting the post-buckling response of a composite beam with piezoelectric patches connected to a harvesting circuit; the development and investigation of a novel portable demonstrator; and its experimental validation. In the detailed design phase, highlights of the numerical methodology include the development of a layerwise shell FE model in COMSOL, capable of simulating the coupled nonlinear electromechanical vibration response of the beam throughout pre- and postbuckling, while been connected to a typical in-house harvesting circuit comprising low-power electronics. In the testing phase, the main highlight is related to the comparison of performance of the single specimen for energy harvesting and the PEH demonstrator: Tonal vibration tests are presented on two experimental set-ups serving verification of the model and quantification of power output of the PEH in ground test operating conditions. As will be shown, the PEH complied to the requirements set by the operator, indicating promising potential towards successful implementation in wind turbine blades.

sections.heading: 2. Design of the bistable PEH
sections.text: The design of the PEH is based on numerical models and experimental verification. Some basic design choices have been dictated by the requirements set of the specific application, which is harvesting of mechanical energy from vibrations existing in a wind turbine blade [16]. The electromechanical part of the PEH and the harvesting circuit were modeled in Comsol Multiphysics [45]. Simulation for design involved two separate parts: (i) the piezoelectric beam under compression coupled with the harvesting circuit and (ii) the supporting frame for the axial compression to be applied. In the following, the various design steps are outlined on a sequential basis.

sections.heading: 2.1. Specific design requirements
sections.text: The PEH will be installed inside a wind turbine blade. Specific requirements raise from such an implementation perspective. Wind turbine blades vibrate during operation in a lowfrequency excitation range induced by aerodynamic and inertia loads. Depending on the blade configuration, the base excitation of the harvester during operation is expected to lie in a broad frequency range up to $1 5 \ \mathrm { H z }$ . Consideration of locally added weight constraints should be also taken into account in the design process, aiming at achieving minimum effect on the aeroelastic performance of the blade and preserving safe operation. Since the objective of applying a PEH in a wind turbine blade is the elimination of the need to replace batteries in electronic devices installed in the blade, resilience of the harvester is also required in order to ensure seamless operation within the service life of the blade. Adaptability to specialty installation constraints and extensibility to feed various power source demand are additional key objectives of a welldesigned demonstrator. Table 1 summarizes the main requirements set by the specific application of the harvester.

sections.heading: 2.2. Conceptual design
sections.text:
The concept of the PEH demonstrator is illustrated in figure 1. The electromechanical energy conversion is derived from the strain developed on two piezoelectric transducers bonded at the middle of a composite beam in post-buckling, which is subjected to a base acceleration. The post-buckling of the beam is achieved by means of a supporting lightweight steel frame and an axial compression mechanism. The piezoelectric transducers are connected to a harvesting circuit. An in-house developed harvesting circuit is considered for validation of the functional principle and the simulation model.

The harvester is analyzed into three interacting subassemblies: a mechanical for structural support, an electromechanical for energy conversion and an electric for energy harvesting. More specifically:

The mechanical subassembly includes the compression mechanism and its supporting frame. The mechanism is composed of a $\mu \mathrm { m }$ -resolution thread screw and sheet- metal

clamps assembled with screws in tight tolerance with the frame.   
• The electromechanical subassembly consists of a composite beam, axially loaded in compression up to post buckling regime, and two piezoelectric transducers, symmetrically placed at center with respect to beam thickness, which are connected to a PEH circuit.   
• The electric subassembly comprises the harvesting circuit, which is connected to the electromechanical subassembly at the terminals of the piezoelectric transducers.

sections.heading: 2.3. Detailed design
sections.text:
The sizing of the mechanical subassembly rests on feedback from dynamic measurements of prestressed beams on a lab experimental setup. It is performed by developing two independent FE models: (i) a coupled electromechanical model for simulating the closed-circuit response of the piezoelectric transducers connected with the harvesting circuit and (ii) a mechanical model for the supporting frame. 2.3.1. Electromechanical subassembly. The studied electromechanical system for mechanical vibration energy conversion comprises of a beam with piezoelectric patches, shown in figure 2. The piezoelectric patches have been bonded at the center of the span on top and bottom faces. Additional masses have been glued on the beam faces at symmetric locations along the $x y$ -plane. Table 2 lists the geometrical parameters of the electromechanical design. The beam was sized to be in post-buckling regime at an axial load of $3 0 0 { - } 4 0 0 \ \mathrm { N }$ (table 1) without plastic deformation. The axial load has been selected in this range, which may seem quite high, since preliminary designs and tests indicated that the beam, including piezoelectric patch with tuned thickness, should not be too compliant in order to achieve sufficient power according to design requirements, as also observed by other researchers [46, 47]. Composite material was selected for the beam, since it ensures optimal stiffness/weight ratio and linear elastic performance for the studied strain levels. In addition, its fatigue endurance is expected to exceed those of metallic materials based on typical measurements on composites. DuraAct P876.A11 [48] piezoelectric patches were selected, which offer large deformation capabilities and include piezoceramic material, which exceeds piezopolymers in electromechanical power conversion at the studied strains. Based on sensitivity studies on the effect of concentrated mass, excitation frequency and base acceleration on harvested power, a total mass of $2 9 0 ~ \mathrm { g }$ was bonded symmetrically on both sides at the center of the span. In table 3 the electromechanical properties of composite and piezoelectric material of the harvester are listed. 2.3.2. Electric subassembly. An in-house harvesting circuit (cc-ih), illustrated in figure 3, was used for model validation and mechanical design improvement towards implementation of commercial harvesting circuits in field-operation [49]. It could be modeled approximately, as most parameters were provided by the component manufacturers. It includes three main parts: a rectifier, a charging capacitor, and a discharging switch (MOSFET), all connected to the piezoelectric current sources. A resistive load is connected to the MOSFET for ease of harvested power measurement, whereas different kinds of loads, including batteries, can be powered. Table 1. Calculating the displacement vector $\pmb { u }$ and the charge vector $\tilde { \boldsymbol { Q } } ^ { f }$ from equation (7), along with their time derivatives, the electric potential is calculated as, $$ t _ { \tilde { \varphi } ^ { f } = [ R ] } t \dot { \tilde { Q } } ^ { f } $$ where $\dot { \tilde { Q } } ^ { f }$ represents the electric current from the piezoelectric terminal to the external resistive load $R$ . The system of equation (7) describes the forced harmonic response in the case of a shunted resistance. In the case of a more complex load, this equation can be formulated using the load impedance. In the general case of an arbitrary harvesting circuit, as in the current work, this can be addressed by exploiting the capabilities of COMSOL in modeling circuit components. Thus, the present continuum model in COMSOL provides a solution for the electromechanical system coupled with the PEH circuit in one shot. The solution procedure is shown in figure 6 and basically requires two steps: A static step is employed first to account for the application of prestress by an induced axial displacement at the beam’s free end. This is then followed by a time-dependent solution accounting for the application of an acceleration at the base. A modal solution may be also implemented for deriving the modal frequencies of the prestressed beam after the static solution. The static solver implemented is based on a damped Newton’s nonlinear method [52], whereas a backward Euler differentiation formula [53] is used in the time-dependent solver and the implicitly restarted Arnoldi method in the modal solver [54]. As reported in the previous section, a harvesting circuit consists of an input/charging and an output/discharging branch. The harvested power from the PEH circuit is calculated using the energy guided to the output of the discharging subcircuit between two timestamps as, $$ P \left( t \right) = \frac { \int _ { t _ { 1 } } ^ { t _ { 2 } } \tilde { \varphi } \left( t \right) \dot { \tilde { Q } } ^ { f } \left( t \right) \mathrm { d } t } { t _ { 2 } - t _ { 1 } } . $$ 2.3.4. Supporting frame model. The FE discretization of the supporting frame includes beam and shell elements. Numerical and experimental studies, presented in section 4.1, indicated that an axial displacement of $5 0 - 5 5 \ \mu \mathrm { m }$ is required at the free end of the beam in order to get it to postbuckling regime. The corresponding axial compressive force is in the range of $2 0 0 { - } 3 0 0 \ \mathrm { N }$ . Figure 7 illustrates the distribution of total displacement and von Mises stress on the steel frame of the mechanical subassembly in the case of an applied reaction force of $3 0 0 \mathrm { ~ N ~ }$ outwards at each side of the frame. The modeling for design procedure of the frame resulted in a quadratic cross section beam profile of $1 \ \mathrm { m m }$ side length and a shell thickness of $1 ~ \mathrm { m m }$ for the bottom/top sheets. The plates supporting the axial compression mechanism were sized $3 ~ \mathrm { \ m m }$ thick to ensure adequately small outward $x$ -displacement. The selected dimensions ensure a maximum stress of ${ 5 0 } \mathrm { M P a }$ . The weight derived by the mechanical subsystem modelling process is $0 . 5 4 \mathrm { k g }$ . ![](images/6e8e176ec2cbb4223cface81de2313eb6b5641ae9659140c93677c8de544240a.jpg) Figure 5. Solution flowchart of the coupled electromechanical model.

sections.heading: 3. Physical prototypes and testing procedures
sections.text:
Two experimental configurations were set up to serve verification of the simulated response of the vibrating specimen with the harvesting circuit, and testing of the full

PEH demonstrator, respectively. This testing strategy enabled measurement of compressive force and applied axial displacement at one end of the specimen in the former case. In the latter case, post-buckling of the specimen was traced by measuring the fundamental modal frequency of the specimen in the supporting frame at non-measured force and axial displacement conditions. Both procedures, along with physical prototype manufacturing details, are schematically shown in figure 8 and described in the next sections.

![](images/4f614db5369a789c4fbd3c3e04eb4b12de029904838d58706e1ed954c5eaf09d.jpg)  
Figure 7. FE results of the frame supporting the axial compression mechanism: (a)–(b) total displacement of shells and beams, respectively, (c)–(d) von Mises stress.

![](images/66b3d1e6cbf677873ff05c9bec2758f29e4b7821a7a304dedc922e57d3282f01.jpg)

![](images/9c7451bef079a78f4d1d3ed71831691c46281ed7a62b29f7bf0d9bc33e1d29a9.jpg)

sections.heading: 3.1. Axially prestressed beam with harvesting circuit
sections.text:
A composite beam of Glass/Epoxy material with surfaceattached piezoceramic films and a symmetric balanced $[ 9 0 _ { 2 } / 0 _ { 4 } / 9 0 _ { 2 } ]$ lamination was studied. The specimens were fabricated by vacuum-assisted hand lay-up and cured in environmental conditions $( T = 2 5 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ , moisture $= 4 5 \%$ ). The elastic properties of the composite laminate have been determined experimentally via modal analysis tests under free–free boundary conditions, following the same procedure as in [55]. The hand layup fabrication process does not ensure equal thickness per composite ply and no unique thickness along the length of the specimen. To stimulate stable buckling in the numerical model, as was observed in the experiments, each lower $9 0 ^ { \circ }$ plies were assumed to have a thickness of $0 . 3 7 5 \mathrm { m m }$ while each upper one was assumed being $0 . 2 5 \mathrm { m m }$ thick. The total thickness of the composite specimen was measured to be $2 . 5 \mathrm { m m }$ at average, as shown in table 2.

The experimental setup designed for enabling dynamic vibrations of axially prestressed beams is displayed in figure 9. It consists of a horizontal aluminum platform, capable to oscillate laterally on a pair of linear guide rails. Two steel corner brackets were used to provide the clamped boundary conditions at both ends of the beam specimen. The left corner bracket is fixed on the base platform and is connected with the left grip. At the other end, the right grip is bonded on the platform via a micrometer stage providing the horizontal axial displacement to the specimen. The right end is additionally equipped with a static load cell (1102–04 A model from PCB Piezotronics) capable of measuring the resulting axial compressive force generated to the right grip due to the applied displacement. After imposition of axial displacement, the specimen was fixed between the two grips and its static deflection was measured by a laser vibrometer.

The whole setup could oscillate laterally via an electromechanical shaker conjoined with its horizontal platform. A dynamic load cell, connected in series between the shaker and the platform, recorded the reaction force from the shaker to the base. An accelerometer attached on the platform and another one connected to the center of the beam specimen measured simultaneously the base and specimen acceleration, respectively. The resulting difference between the two accelerations provided the net acceleration signal at the center of the beam with respect to its supports. A DAQ board was used to simultaneously acquire the signals from all sensors, and the frequency response function of the measured specimen acceleration versus the applied force on the frame was extracted.

sections.heading: 3.2. Full PEH demonstrator
sections.text:
The PEH demonstrator is shown in figure 10. The steel frame and the clamps of the mechanical subassembly were manufactured using sheet metal laser cutting and strand forming, and a $\mu \mathrm { m }$ -thread screw was used for the compression mechanism. The mechanical frame was mounted on the testing platform described in section 3.1 and the same sensors were used except the micrometer and the specimen load cell. Lacking these two sensors, the testing procedure was performed in two steps:

First, the post-buckling regime of the beam was determined by studying its modal frequency from the measured FRFs, which is affected by the applied axial compressive load. At buckling, the modal frequency is minimal and rises at higher load [56]. The modal frequency was measured by analyzing the FRF of the beam under white-noise base excitation $( 0 -$ $2 0 0 \mathrm { H z }$ ). Since no axial displacement or force is measured, the prestress level can be derived by measuring the static deflection at the center of the beam by the non-contact laser LVDT.

![](images/6ee7469fc1622d43fe8f69bea9b274ae4ef3f2a755b02c6c1776f7b34c3ee8c0.jpg)  
Figure 10. PEH demonstrator under test: (i) close-up of original configuration, (ii) overview of test bench to present non-contact laser LVDT.

• At a second step, which is the step of dynamic response and harvesting, the beam was subjected to a sinusoidal base excitation at $8 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ with oscillatory amplitude ideally selected in order to generate approximately $_ { 1 \mathrm { ~ g ~ } }$ acceleration on the specimen. The values of frequency and acceleration considered are typical of the excitation induced on wind turbine blades in operation.

sections.heading: 4.1. Modal frequency identification tests under prestress
sections.text:
As a first step, the COMSOL FE model of the beam in opencircuit conditions was validated against numerical predictions of an in-house FE software [51] and measurements of static buckling response and modal analysis tests performed on the testing configuration described in section 3.1. The in-house FE is a 9-node Lagrange shell FE based on first-order single-layer shear theory kinematics.

Figure 11(a) shows predicted and measured static buckling response in terms of axial force vs lateral displacement (deflection), whereas figure 11(b) shows the simulated and measured effect of axial prestressing force on linearized first modal frequency. While sufficiently following the measured curve, the COMSOL model predicts buckling at a lower load compared to the measured one. In addition, the physical specimen appears to follow a more stable pre-buckling path than in both simulations, approaching buckling more gradually. The measured critical buckling load is $2 3 2 . 5 \mathrm { N }$ . The in-house FE overpredicts the measured buckling load at $2 5 8 . 5 \mathrm { N }$ , whereas Comsol predicts buckling at $2 3 0 . 5 \mathrm { N }$ . The deviations between model predictions and measurements indicate that the physical specimen entails additional imperfections and asymmetries not included in the modeled systems. The previous differences in critical buckling loads and pre-buckling path stability are also depicted in the predicted and measured fundamental modal frequency in figure 11(b). Considering that the material properties included in the model have been extracted by modal testing and thus coincide with those of the physical system, these deviations are attributed to: (i) specimen geometric imperfections, such as, uneven specimen thickness and uneven thickness distribution across the layers (composite plies, adhesive) and (ii) different boundary conditions between model and tests, especially in the vicinity of buckling. Both of these deviations got enhanced by the high buckling load required due to relatively high thickness of the specimen $( h _ { t o t a l } = 2 . 7 \ \mathrm { m m }$ at the center), so as to achieve higher strains at high prestress levels and harvest power in the range of $\mathrm { m W } .$ This conclusion is justified when considering the small deviations observed between the in-house FE model and tests in the case of a much thinner specimen [51], which however resulted in harvesting power in the $\mu \mathrm { W }$ range.

Figure 12 illustrates similar measurements of the first modal frequency at small-amplitude excitation versus lateral displacement in the full PEH testing configuration described in section 3.2. The specimen remains at open-circuit conditions and thus no power is harvested at this stage. However, the curve presented in figure 12 reveals the prestress levels to be studied for power harvesting by means of dynamic tests under sinusoidal base excitation. It may be thus characterized as a ‘calibration’ procedure of the harvester, serving the identification of the most promising prestress levels for highest power extraction. These levels may be then verified by phase plots extracted from simulation and/or measured accelerations, indicating inter- or intra-well oscillations in the transient response of the specimen in connection with the harvesting circuit, as presented in the following section. The level of maximum harvested power is in a modal frequency range near $2 0 \mathrm { H z }$ , as shown in the dynamic measurements of table 5. Beyond this point, intrawell oscillation prevails and the harvested power drops drastically.

![](images/5f678f7c8854edada8bd53b4e3d4bb0d25429444893da9f67fbeba97338eb567.jpg)  
Figure 11. Measurements and FE predictions of the single beam response under various prestress levels: (a) static axial force vs lateral displacement, (b) fundamental modal frequency vs axial force.

sections.heading: 4.2. Transient response at various post-buckling sub-regimes
sections.text:
Dynamic tests were performed on both single beam and full PEH at the prestress levels identified from the calibration process. At each dynamic test, a sinusoidal base acceleration of $_ { 1 \mathrm { ~ g ~ } }$ was applied at an excitation frequency of $8 \ \mathrm { H z }$ . A mass of $2 8 7 ~ \mathrm { g }$ was bonded at the centre of the specimen. Tables 4 and 5 show FE simulation results and measurements of harvested power for various levels of axial compressive prestress of each system, respectively. The FE model is the same for both systems. Its predictions are presented separately in each table to indicate matching simulated axial displacement with prestress level. The matching was based on measurements related to prestress, which were either the axial compressive force (table 4) or the first modal frequency (table 5), depending on the available measured data. Regarding computational time, for a system with 8055 structural and 1050 electric degrees of freedom, an average computational time of $4 0 \ \mathrm { h }$ is required for 2 s of simulated response on an Intel® core™ i9-10900K CPU $\textcircled { a } 3 . 7 0 \mathrm { G H z }$ with 64 Gb RAM. ![](images/a9c72782d39e9de2165a4282db9484e2d8c308eb55b2df2cba1bee19103a9af5.jpg) Figure 12. Measured effect of prestress, expressed as deflection at center, on modal frequency of composite piezoelectric beam of the PEH demonstrator. In both single beam and full PEH systems three levels of efficiency may be distinguished based on prestress, where the harvesting circuit exhibits low, high, and very low output power, respectively, on the resistance of the discharging sub-circuit. This trend is evidenced in both simulation and test and may be justified by the simulated phase plots shown in figure 13. Bistable interwell response is observed at both $6 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ and $7 5 \mu \mathrm { m }$ axial compressive displacement at free end, whereas at $7 5 \mu \mathrm { m }$ the amplitudes of velocity and deflection are slightly higher. Maximum measured power has been harvested at $8 5 \ \mu \mathrm { { m } }$ in both systems. At no less than $1 2 5 \ \mu \mathrm { m }$ simulated axial compressive displacement the system gets trapped in intrawell oscillations, which lead to lower power harvesting. By comparing power output of single beam and full PEH configurations it is concluded that the portable harvester generally performs similar to the fixed beam, being however about $10 \% { - } 1 5 \%$ less efficient at high power output levels. In the full PEH (table 5) the maximum measured power is $1 . 3 2 \mathrm { m W }$ at a modal frequency of $2 0 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ , which is simulated by a prestress induced through an axial compressive displacement of $8 5 \mu \mathrm { m }$ at the free end. Shortly after this prestress level there is a sudden drop in measured harvested power, as also observed in the single beam (table 4). The FE model simulation succeeds in capturing this drop at a very high prestress level of $u = 1 4 5 ~ \mu \mathrm { m }$ . This evidence is attributed to deviation in the boundary conditions at the supports of both single beam and full PEH. From the comparison of simulated with measured modal frequencies it can be concluded that the physical beam configuration is more compliant than the simulated within the whole range of applied prestress. This higher compliance is related to rotations allowed at the supports of the demonstrator and overall clearance of the full PEH assembly. At levels of prestress exceeding a modal frequency in the vicinity of $2 0 \mathrm { H z }$ it is reasonably assumed that the deviation in boundary conditions between simulation and test has a dominant effect on the bistable response and therefore the stiffer simulated beam requires a much higher prestress compared to test to reach the drop-off in harvested power. Phase plot of simulated harvester’s transient response for various levels of prestress expressed as axial displacement input in Comsol FE model. Figure 14(a) presents measured and predicted piezoelectric voltage at each patch, and predicted capacitor voltage in the cc-ih at an axial compressive displacement of $6 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { { m } }$ at the free edge. Due to rising voltage at the patches, the capacitor is charged up to a discharge threshold selected to be at $2 . 4 \ \mathrm { V } .$ The two piezoelectric patches yield a response practically equal in amplitude and opposite in phase, as expected due to the deformation of the beam in the first buckling mode, shown in figure 14(b). Acceptable correlation between simulation and test is observed regarding the shape of the response. The timestamp of discharge depends exclusively on prestress for given beam configuration and affects the harvested power, since more discharges in a fixed time interval mean more power. Concerning the simulated response of the output subcircuit of the PEH, part of the electric load appears to be dissipated in the MOSFET when it conducts current, as shown in figure 15, where the simulated time histories of MOSFET voltage and external resistor voltage at the output circuit are plotted. The simulated output voltage at the external resistor is approximately $0 . 6 \mathrm { V }$ lower than measured, as illustrated in figure 16. This deviation between simulated and measured output voltage on the resistor is related to the internal resistance of the MOSFET, which was determined indirectly through other MOSFET parameters. The latter can hardly be found in full detail from datasheets of manufacturers [57] and some of them, e.g. the gate voltage, were thus assumed. By considering the simulated voltage dissipated on the internal MOSFET resistor in the COMSOL model $( \varphi r _ { \mathrm { M O S } } , s )$ , the total simulated output voltage is $2 . 4 \mathrm { V } ,$ as designed and measured. Regarding the timestamps of the discharging spikes occurring in the output circuit (figure 16) as typically observed in harvesting circuits, the comparison between simulated and measured values is considered to be acceptable from a power harvesting design perspective. Both measured and simulated signals do not yield periodicity, as expected from similar lack of periodicity in the case of the input circuit (figure 14). The deviation between predicted and measured discharging timestamp is attributed to discrepancies in boundary conditions and approximations in the simulated harvesting circuit, including its internal resistance which is not modeled. However, these deviations did not seem to drastically affect the accuracy in power harvesting prediction (table 5). The PEH device was measured to harvest power of more than $1 \mathrm { m W }$ thus fulfilling the main design objective set in this study (table 1). ![](images/8bc5e7dc6bb8c0bfa30b4da8f0607ea6908e4f8253ecc308bc26692f1b92e268.jpg) Figure 14. (a) Typical response of piezoelectric transducers at axial compressive displacement of $u = 6 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ , where $\cdot _ { \mathrm { m } } \cdot \mathrm { ~ m } '$ denotes measured and $\cdot _ { s } ,$ simulated data; (b) typical fundamental buckling mode. The enhanced capabilities of the coupled structure-circuit FE model include prediction of both global electric-, as well as, local mechanical parameters. From a design perspective, the addition of a concentrated mass at the midspan of the beam is beneficial for the harvested power, yet practically limited by the compliance of the composite beam and the endurance of the adhesive joint between mass and piezoelectric patch. To this end, optimal design of axially compressed vibrating harvesters is facilitated by the use of FE models, since an anisotropic mechanical continuum approach enables the prediction of mechanical stresses and strains through the thickness of the lamination. Typical through-thickness distributions of interlaminar shear strain and stress in the composite beam model studied herein at maximum static deformation in postbuckling is shown in figure 17. Similar distributions are also developed in the dynamic response. The layerwise kinematic assumptions of equation (4) enable capturing such complex profiles, which provide to the designer an estimation of shear stresses at the interface between dissimilar materials, such as adhesive and piezoelectric patch. Thus, the present model can be used as a detailed-design tool for predicting both harvested power and local stress field for ensuring mechanical fatigue endurance. Though, it should be noted that the increase of discrete layers in the FE model, as for instance by modeling the adhesive, leads to higher computational cost, practically double per additional layer depending on the FE mesh and overall vibration response. ![](images/1a107c15b7dfab17e067635aeced0be4d3451c0d53c76675b6066632422ad85a.jpg) Figure 15. sections.heading: 5. Summary and conclusions
sections.text:
A PEH demonstrator was presented from the design requirements level up to ground test evaluation. Its mechanical, electromechanical and electric subassemblies were designed using coupled mechanical-electric field FE analysis to simulate the bistable dynamic response in the range of specified excitation. Simulation predictions were validated by measurements performed on two physical prototypes: the single beam at post buckling and the full PEH. From these comparisons the following main conclusions can be drawn:

Prestress calibration by means of modal frequency is an essential primary step to achieve operation of the piezoelectric beam at post buckling and thus maximize power harvesting.

• At post-buckling, the harvested power increases with prestress up to a transition point, which mainly depends on the rigidity of the supports and the overall clearance in the mechanical assembly. After this point the power drops off drastically.   
• The full PEH performs similar to the single beam, indicating successful design transfer from functional principle to operating demonstrator for installation.   
The FE model accurately predicts the harvested power and sufficiently captures the bistable dynamic response of the piezoelectric beam at efficient levels of post-buckling, whereas it overestimates the transition point due to poor representation of the physical boundary conditions at high prestress levels.

As the main benefit of the PEH with regards to the design specification, the harvester fulfills all set requirements: Having a weight of $1 . 2 ~ \mathrm { k g }$ , it is capable of producing $1 . 3 2 ~ \mathrm { m W }$ at operating conditions and offers portability and extensibility. It may be considered as a harvesting unit, capable of being extended by applying additional units to increase the harvested power. Resilience is ensured by employing composite material in the harvesting beam to achieve good fatigue endurance, whereas a position locking bolt at the compression mechanism ensures the preservation of axial compressive prestress. The main limitation of the PEH is related to the existence of a maximum prestress level for efficient energy harvesting, which has been estimated to be $2 4 8 . 5 \mathrm { ~ N ~ }$ in the current configuration. Above this prestress level the PEH performance drops drastically. Thus, the PEH should be designed according to the requirements set for the specific application, since the allowable weight drives the maximum prestress applicable to the PEH metallic frame. Future studies will focus on integration of the harvester in self-powered data acquisition and wireless transmission systems, and implementation in wind turbine blades in operation to quantify its on-field performance.
